name: Topsoil (the dark, humus-rich surface horizon under lawn and planting)
summary: The top horizon of a garden soil: mineral grains (sand, silt, clay) mixed with humus from roots and leaf litter, worked by soil life, with pores that hold water and air. It is the ground under the grounds' mown lawn, the meadow and orchard of the Hall of Light's gardens, the hedges' feet and Chenghuai's garden beds, seen where the turf is thin, at the edge of beds and between plants. Nature grows the plants in it; Matter records the soil's own physics.

workings.note: Cultivation (digging, raking, rolling) changes its structure, not its substance; no working record yet.

constituents.role: the finest fraction; holds water and nutrients
darkens the soil and binds its crumbs

constituents.material: water and air in the pores
constituents.role: the live state: wetness is the surface law's

formation.how: Soil forms where rock weathers into mineral grains and plants add organic matter year on year. Under grass, dense fine roots die back into the soil each year and build a thick, dark, humus-rich surface horizon: the soil scientists' mollic epipedon, which is defined by its darkness. A lawn's topsoil is that kind of horizon, or an imported topsoil made to resemble it.

mollicColour.text: A horizon is mollic if, among other criteria, its moist Munsell chroma and value are both 3 or less and its organic carbon is at least 0.6 % (organic matter at least 1.0 %) throughout.
mollicColour.source: University of Georgia, Soil Science, 'A Key to Common Diagnostic Horizons in Soil Taxonomy' (teaching key after the USDA Keys to Soil Taxonomy), item 2 'mollic', https://soils.uga.edu/files/2016/08/A-Key-to-Soil-Orders-and-Common-Diagnostic-Horizons-in-Soil-Taxonomy.pdf

wet.text: Soil reflectance falls non-linearly with moisture, well described by an exponential model, similar for different soils when moisture is expressed as the degree of saturation.
wet.source: D.B. Lobell, G.P. Asner (2002) 'Moisture effects on soil reflectance', Soil Science Society of America Journal 66(3):722-727, https://doi.org/10.2136/sssaj2002.7220 (abstract read at https://asu.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/moisture-effects-on-soil-reflectance/)

wet.text: Wet surfaces are darker because water fills the pores and films the grains, lowering the index step and trapping light by total internal reflection.
wet.source: J. Lekner, M.C. Dorf (1988) 'Why some things are darker when wet', Applied Optics 27(7):1278-1280, https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.27.001278

wet.text: The same physics explains wet-dry reflectance differences in sands and soils.
wet.source: S.A. Twomey, C.F. Bohren, J.L. Mergenthaler (1986) 'Reflectance and albedo differences between wet and dry surfaces', Applied Optics 25(3):431-437, https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.25.000431
wet.note: Qualitative summary; the paper's numbers were not read.

structure.text: A mollic horizon's structure is not massive, or its consistence is not hard when dry: it is crumbly.

absorption.derivation: Normal-incidence absorption 1 - |R|^2 of a semi-infinite ground, R = (Z - 1)/(Z + 1), with the Delany-Bazley normalised impedance Z = 1 + 0.0571 X^-0.754 - i 0.087 X^-0.732, X = rho0 f / sigma, rho0 = 1.204 kg/m3, at the class's representative flow resistivity sigma. photograph: Very dark brown to near black when damp, dusty grey-brown when the top dries.
Crumbly, with fine roots, grit and bits of leaf; a paler dry crust after sun, cracked on clayey soil.
Under a lawn it shows only in thin patches and at cut edges; along a bed's edge a clean cut line.
Crumbs and clods from millimetres to centimetres, sand grains and plant litter at the surface.

unverified.reason: No measured reflectance of a humus-rich topsoil was read. Textbook albedo tables (Oke 1987, 'Boundary Layer Climates', Table 1.1) give ranges for dark wet and light dry soils; not read at the source.
Munsell value 3 corresponds to a luminous reflectance of roughly 6-7 % by the Munsell renotation (ASTM D1535); the conversion was not read at a source.
Lobell and Asner's fitted amplitude, rate and minimum for each soil were not read (abstract only).
The textbook 'about 45 % mineral, 5 % organic matter, 25 % water, 25 % air' for an ideal loam was not read at a source.

The old build's lawn ground tone (0.05, 0.072, 0.026) linear (windows/Scripts/lawn.py) and GardenGround #49492F (windows/Scripts/chenghuai.py), chosen by eye: they include thatch and moss, not soil alone.
